title: Stop guessing at responsive bugs. Measure them.
excerpt: A 94px overflow, a 2px double border, and four measurement traps that will each give you a confidently wrong answer.
content:
Most layout bugs are not where they look. I relearned that on my own portfolio, where a stray 1px line under the header, a column of text crushed down to one word per line, and a code block quietly scrolling sideways all turned out to be somewhere other than where I first went looking.

So I stopped re-reading my CSS and started measuring the page in a real browser instead.

## The bug that started all of this

My mobile menu left a thin bordered strip under the header on every single page. The menu collapsed with a max-height of zero and overflow hidden, which should have made it disappear completely.

It did hide the content. But the panel still carried a border-top and a border-bottom, and a zero-height box with borders still paints. So the collapsed panel rendered as a 2px-tall bordered rectangle sitting directly on top of the header's own 1px bottom border.

Three pixels of line with an empty gap trapped inside it. Exactly the kind of thing you can see clearly and explain not at all.

The fix was not to adjust a border colour. It was to decide who owns that boundary. The panel draws no border at all now, and the last item in its list draws the closing line. One boundary, one owner, every time.

## Four ways to measure the wrong thing

I wrote a short script that drives headless Chrome across every route at sixteen widths. It found far more than I expected, but only after I fixed the measurement itself. Each of these four gave me a confident and wrong answer.

## scrollWidth is clamped to clientWidth

This one cost me the most time. If you check whether content fits by comparing scrollWidth against clientWidth, the answer is always yes, even when it overflows by 94px. scrollWidth never reports less than clientWidth, so that comparison can never fail.

To get the real overflow you have to walk the line boxes instead: take a Range over the element's contents, group the resulting rects by their top edge, and compare the widest one against the content box edge.

## getClientRects on a block returns one rect

You might reasonably expect one rect per line. On a block element you get a single rect, which is the border box. If your line-counting logic reports one for a twelve-line paragraph, this is why. Use a Range over the contents, not the element itself.

## Overflows the viewport is not the page scrolls

These are different failures with different fixes, and conflating them sends you chasing the wrong element. Check the document's scrollWidth against innerWidth separately. Content inside an overflow: auto container legitimately extends past the viewport while the page itself stays perfectly still.

## When one axis scrolls, the other follows

I set overflow-y to auto on a code panel and never asked for horizontal scrolling. The spec hands it to me anyway: when one axis is not visible, visible on the other axis computes to auto. So the panel scrolled sideways, silently, behind a scrollbar I never designed.

## The numbers that actually settled it

For the code panel on my contact page I finally measured the line boxes and compared the widest line against the pane's content box:

- at 1280px the longest line needed 458px and the pane offered 372px, a 94px spill
- at 1440px it was still 62px over
- at 1600px it fit, with 19px to spare

That gave me the real constraint. Not the font is too big, but this line needs about 430px of content box and the pane only has 372. No amount of padding tweaking was ever going to close that gap.

So I changed the markup instead. A flat paragraph full of line breaks needs white-space nowrap to keep its shape, and that is precisely what forced the overflow. One flex row per line, with a fixed-width gutter for the line number and a min-width zero cell for the code, lets a line wrap inside its own box. The wrapped part now stays aligned under the code rather than under the line number, and nothing can escape the pane at any width.

## Two things that only look broken

Rule these out before you change a single line. I nearly rewrote perfectly good code because of both of them.

- Decorative bleed. Blurred glow blobs positioned partly off-screen are intentional. If the page's scrollWidth still equals innerWidth, the container is clipping them and there is no bug to fix.
- Transform animations. A ping-style animation changes an element's bounding box without touching layout at all. Check the computed animation name before you flag it.

## What I would tell you to do

- Measure first. One number settles in a single call what guessing will not settle in ten.
- Give every boundary exactly one owner. If two elements can both draw the same line, one day they will.
- Assert on the property you actually mean. I checked transform on an element that was rotated with the standalone rotate property, and concluded that a perfectly working arrow was broken.
- Keep the script. Mine is about thirty lines, and it will catch the next regression before a visitor does.

title: The React StrictMode bug that looked like a browser glitch
excerpt: My typing animation kept stalling halfway and needed a refresh to recover. The cause was a one-character flaw in a library's effect cleanup.
content:
Sometimes the typing animation on my home page would stop halfway through my own name. Part of a word, then nothing. A refresh fixed it, which is the worst kind of bug report, because it works now is not a diagnosis.

So I ran the page twelve times in a row and counted. It failed twelve times out of twelve. It was never intermittent. It only looked that way because I kept refreshing instead of watching.

## What the animation actually did

Three lines type out in sequence: a greeting, my name, then my role. Each one starts when the previous one finishes. The chain is what broke. The first line stopped mid-word, so the callback meant to start the second line never fired, and the third line never appeared at all.

The animation came from a small React wrapper around a popular typing library. The wrapper looked completely reasonable, and that was exactly the problem.

## The one character that broke it

The wrapper's setup effect ended with something equivalent to this: take the current instance if there is one, update its options, and if that returned nothing, build a fresh instance instead. Written as a fallback expression, it reads naturally.

But updating the options does not return nothing. It returns the instance. An object is always truthy, so the branch that builds a new instance could only ever run while the reference was still empty.

Now add React StrictMode, which mounts a component, runs its cleanup, and mounts it again. The cleanup called the library's destroy method but never cleared the reference. So on the second mount the effect found a reference to an instance that had already been destroyed, decided it was fine, updated its options, and never created a working one.

Nothing typed. The completion callback never fired. The whole sequence stalled, exactly as reported.

## Then I made it worse

My first fix was to drop the wrapper and drive the library's core directly, calling destroy myself and clearing the reference so the second mount would build a fresh instance.

It failed twelve times out of twelve again, but differently. This time the characters came out doubled: the name typed itself twice, interleaved, one character at a time.

The core schedules its work on animation frames, and its destroy method only clears pending timeouts. It does not stop the animation frame loop, and that loop has no guard telling it that it has been destroyed. The mount, cleanup, mount cycle therefore left a second live loop writing into the same element as the first. Two writers, one DOM node, doubled output.

## Owning the timer myself

The fix was to stop fighting the library and write the thirty lines myself. A plain timeout chain, one writer per mount, a cancelled flag, and a cleanup that clears the timer and empties the element. No animation frames, no instance to reuse, nothing that can double up.

It has since run clean twelve times out of twelve on a cold load, and eight out of eight when I navigate away and come back, which is the case that broke it in the first place.

## What I took from it

- Reproduce before you fix. Twelve runs turned sometimes into always, and that is a completely different problem to solve.
- A test that cannot fail is not a test. My first check passed while the page was visibly broken, because I was asserting on the wrong element. Asserting on the final text of all three lines made the failure obvious.
- StrictMode is a gift, not a nuisance. It forces you to notice that a dependency's cleanup does not actually clean up. In production this would have stayed intermittent and I would have kept blaming the browser.
- Do not fight a dependency that refuses to clean up after itself. If the fix is thirty lines, those thirty lines are cheaper than the workaround.
- Put decorative glyphs in CSS, not in the DOM. The blinking cursor was a span containing a pipe character, so the element's text content read as my name followed by a pipe. Screen readers announced it, copy and paste picked it up, and my own assertion against the exact title failed. Moving the glyph into a CSS pseudo-element fixed all three at once.
